prompt: A food worker with a stomach bug handles lettuce without washing their hands, and customers who eat it get sick. Which link in the chain of infection is the contaminated lettuce?

options.text: Portal of exit
options.feedback: The portal of exit is how the germ leaves the worker, such as through hands or stool.

options.text: Vehicle (how the germ travels from the reservoir to a new host)
options.feedback: Right: the lettuce carries the germ from the sick worker to customers. Stopping the vehicle breaks the chain.

options.text: Reservoir (where the germ normally lives)
options.feedback: The reservoir here is the sick worker. The lettuce is how the germ moves.

options.text: Susceptible host
options.feedback: The customers are the susceptible hosts. The lettuce is not a person.

explanation: The chain of infection has six links: germ, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission (the vehicle or route), portal of entry, and susceptible host. Break any link and the chain stops.
hint: Ask: what moves the germ between people?

prompt: A public pool's water carries a germ from one swimmer's illness to many other swimmers. Which link in the chain of infection is the pool water?

options.text: Vehicle (how the germ travels to a new host)
options.feedback: Yes: the pool water carries the germ from the reservoir to new hosts.

options.text: Reservoir
options.feedback: The reservoir is the original source, such as a sick swimmer. The water carries the germ onward.

options.text: Susceptible host
options.feedback: The swimmers who get sick are the hosts.

options.text: Portal of entry
options.feedback: The portal of entry is how the germ gets into the new host's body, such as swallowing water.

explanation: The pool water is the vehicle: it carries the germ from where it came from to new hosts. Public health acts on whichever link is easiest to break.
hint: Ask: what moves the germ between people?

prompt: Riverton's lab reports show 40 confirmed stomach-illness cases this week. Why are there probably many more people who are actually sick?

options.text: Only a fraction of sick people seek care, get tested, and are reported, so reported cases are the tip of the iceberg.
options.feedback: Yes: this is the surveillance pyramid. Many ill people stay home, are never tested, or are never reported.

options.text: The lab made counting errors.
options.feedback: Lab errors exist but are small. The big gap comes from people never being tested.

options.text: Everyone who gets sick is reported, so 40 is the true number.
options.feedback: Reports only count people who reach the system. Most illness goes uncounted.

options.text: The extra cases are people who were not really sick.
options.feedback: Nothing in the data says that. The undercount is real illness that never reached a lab.

explanation: Surveillance systems see only cases that move up the pyramid: illness, then care, then testing, then reporting. Each step loses people.
hint: Think about how many sick people actually get tested.

prompt: A county reports 25 confirmed cases of a stomach bug. A survey of households finds that about 600 residents had the same symptoms. What best explains the difference?

options.text: Households exaggerate their symptoms.
options.feedback: Surveys have error, but a 24-fold gap is mostly explained by who reaches the testing system.

options.text: Surveillance counts every case, so the survey must be wrong.
options.feedback: Surveillance systems know they miss cases; they are built to detect trends, not count every illness.

options.text: Cases reported are always larger than true illness.
options.feedback: Reported cases are almost always smaller than true illness.

options.text: Most ill people never see a doctor or get tested, so reports count only part of the illness.
options.feedback: Right: underreporting is normal in surveillance, which is why investigators add active case finding.

explanation: Reported counts are a small, delayed sample of the true illness. That is why active case finding exists.
hint: Think about how many sick people actually get tested.

prompt: Why do surveillance reports often lag several days behind when people actually got sick?

options.text: Care-seeking, lab testing, and paperwork all take time before a case is reported.
options.feedback: Yes: the delay is built in, so the newest days look artificially low on the report.

options.text: People wait to get sick until the health department asks them to.
options.feedback: Illness starts on its own schedule. Reporting is what lags.

options.text: Reports are only sent once a month by law.
options.feedback: Many systems report daily or weekly. The delay comes from the process, not the calendar.

options.text: Delays happen only when there is an error.
options.feedback: Delay is normal, even when everything works.

explanation: There is a lag between onset and report. The newest days on a surveillance chart look low until cases are reported.
hint: Think about how long a lab result takes.

prompt: A health department sees that reported cases fell sharply on the most recent two days of its chart. What should an investigator suspect first?

options.text: The outbreak has ended.
options.feedback: It might have, but a drop in the last days is expected from lag alone.

options.text: People stopped getting sick because of media coverage.
options.feedback: Possible, but check reporting delay before drawing that conclusion.

options.text: The lab is hiding cases.
options.feedback: Nothing suggests that. Lag is the usual cause.

options.text: Reporting delay: the latest days are incomplete because not all cases have been reported yet.
options.feedback: Right: recent days often fill in later. Do not assume the outbreak is over.

explanation: A drop at the end of a surveillance chart is often just reporting delay.
hint: Think about how long a lab result takes.

prompt: An investigator defines a case as 'anyone in Riverton with any symptom since last month.' What is the main problem?

options.text: It has no problem: more cases are always better.
options.feedback: More is not better. Non-cases dilute the signal and hide the true exposure.

options.text: It leaves out time, but nothing else.
options.feedback: Time is missing, but so are place, person, and a specific symptom set.

options.text: It is too broad: it counts many people with colds or other illnesses (low specificity).
options.feedback: Yes: a broad definition sweeps in non-cases and makes it hard to see what the outbreak really is.

options.text: It is too narrow: it will miss real cases.
options.feedback: This definition is very inclusive, so it catches nearly everyone. The problem is too many false cases.

explanation: A case definition uses person, place, time, and clinical criteria. Sensitivity is catching true cases; specificity is excluding non-cases. Early on, investigators use a broader definition.
hint: Ask: who would this definition leave out, or let in by mistake?

prompt: A definition says 'a case must have diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and a headache, and live in one neighborhood.' What is the likely result?

options.text: It cannot be evaluated.
options.feedback: You can evaluate it by checking how many true cases it catches (sensitivity).

options.text: It is too narrow: it will miss many true cases (low sensitivity).
options.feedback: Right: requiring every symptom and one place excludes real cases.

options.text: It is too broad: it will include healthy people.
options.feedback: The opposite: it excludes people who are ill.

options.text: It is perfect: stricter is always more accurate.
options.feedback: Strict definitions improve specificity but lose cases and can hide the outbreak's true size.

explanation: Too many criteria drop real cases (low sensitivity). Too few let non-cases in (low specificity).
hint: Ask: who would this definition leave out, or let in by mistake?

prompt: Why do investigators include person, place, and time in a case definition, not just symptoms?

options.text: Because symptoms are unimportant.
options.feedback: Symptoms matter. They work together with person, place, and time.

options.text: Because only place matters in outbreaks.
options.feedback: All of person, place, and time help separate outbreak cases from background illness.

options.text: Because many illnesses share symptoms. Place and time link cases to the same outbreak.
options.feedback: Yes: a bug can cause the same symptoms any day, so time and place focus on this outbreak.

options.text: To make the definition longer and more official.
options.feedback: Length does not improve accuracy. Each element has a job.

explanation: Time, place, person, and symptoms together tie cases to the outbreak instead of everyday illness.
hint: Think about what makes these cases different from everyday illness.

prompt: Stomach illness is common all year. Which addition best helps separate outbreak cases from ordinary background illness?

options.text: Add the person's favorite food.
options.feedback: Favorite foods are not a case criterion. Exposures are studied after cases are defined.

options.text: Limit to people who got sick during the recent period and were linked to the area of concern.
options.feedback: Yes: time and place narrow the case to this outbreak.

options.text: Remove all symptoms from the definition.
options.feedback: Without symptoms you cannot tell stomach illness from anything else.

options.text: Count only the people who live farthest from the area.
options.feedback: That moves away from the likely source.

explanation: Because background illness is always happening, time and place focus the definition on the outbreak.
hint: Think about what makes these cases different from everyday illness.

prompt: An epidemic curve shows one sharp peak with most cases within about 3 days, then almost none. What does this shape suggest?

options.text: The outbreak is still growing.
options.feedback: A sharp peak that drops fast means exposure has ended.

options.text: A point source: many people were exposed at about the same time, such as one meal or event.
options.feedback: Yes: one narrow peak means a single, brief exposure.

options.text: A continuous source: people were exposed over many days.
options.feedback: A continuous source gives a long plateau, not one sharp peak.

options.text: Person-to-person spread in waves.
options.feedback: Waves show repeated peaks about one incubation period apart.

explanation: Point source: one sharp peak. Continuous source: a long plateau. Propagated (person-to-person): successive waves about one incubation period apart.
hint: Look at how wide the peak is.

prompt: An epi curve rises quickly, then stays high for about two weeks before declining slowly. What does this shape suggest?

options.text: A continuous source: people kept being exposed, such as contaminated water or a pool.
options.feedback: Right: the plateau reflects ongoing exposure until the source is removed.

options.text: A point source from a single meal.
options.feedback: A single meal makes a narrow peak that ends within a few incubation periods.

options.text: Person-to-person spread in waves.
options.feedback: Waves show distinct repeated peaks.

options.text: A data error.
options.feedback: A broad plateau is a normal pattern for a continuing source.

explanation: The shape of the curve reflects how long people were exposed.
hint: Look at how wide the peak is.

prompt: An epi curve shows a small first peak, then a bigger peak about three days later, then a third. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Reporting delay only.
options.feedback: Delay shifts the curve; it does not create several separate peaks.

options.text: Propagated spread: each wave of cases infects the next, one incubation period later.
options.feedback: Yes: repeating waves, spaced by about one incubation period, point to person-to-person spread.

options.text: A single meal at an event.
options.feedback: That gives one peak, not repeated waves.

options.text: A continuous source with no pattern.
options.feedback: A continuous source gives a plateau, not separate waves.

explanation: Repeating waves, spaced about one incubation period apart, show that sick people are infecting others.
hint: Count the peaks and look at the gaps.

prompt: A curve for a nursing home shows waves of illness each about 2 to 3 days apart. Which transmission type fits best?

options.text: Propagated: person-to-person spread through the facility.
options.feedback: Right: waves spaced like the incubation period show spread from case to case.

options.text: Point source: one contaminated meal.
options.feedback: One meal produces a single peak.

options.text: Continuous source: a contaminated water supply.
options.feedback: A continuous source gives a plateau.

options.text: Not enough information at all.
options.feedback: The shape itself is informative.

explanation: Successive waves mean cases are generating more cases.
hint: Count the peaks and look at the gaps.

prompt: At a picnic, 60 people ate the potato salad and 24 got sick. What is the attack rate for people who ate the potato salad?

options.feedback: 60 is the number exposed. Divide cases by that, not the other way around.
That divides 1 by 40. Use cases divided by people exposed.
Right: attack rate = ill among those exposed divided by everyone exposed.
24 is the number of cases, not a percent. Divide by the number who ate it (60).

explanation: Attack rate = number who became ill ÷ number at risk, shown as a percent. It is the proportion who got sick, not the count.
hint: Divide cases by the number of people who were at risk.

prompt: In one school class of 25 students, 10 became ill during an outbreak. What is the attack rate for the class?

options.feedback: A rate cannot exceed 100%. Divide cases by people at risk.
Right: cases divided by everyone at risk.
10 is the count of cases, not a rate.
25 is the class size.

explanation: Divide the number ill by the number exposed.
hint: Divide cases by the number of people who were at risk.

prompt: The attack rate is 50% for people who ate the chicken and 5% for people who did not. What is the relative risk and what does it mean?

options.text: RR = 0.1: people who ate chicken were less likely to get sick.
options.feedback: That divides the wrong way around (unexposed over exposed).

options.text: RR = 1: no association.
options.feedback: An RR of 1 means equal risk. Here the exposed had a much higher attack rate.

options.text: RR = 10: people who ate the chicken were 10 times as likely to get sick.
options.feedback: Yes: relative risk compares the attack rate in the exposed to the unexposed. 50 ÷ 5 = 10.

options.text: RR = 45: the difference between 50% and 5%.
options.feedback: That subtracts. Relative risk divides the two attack rates.

explanation: Relative risk = attack rate in the exposed ÷ attack rate in the unexposed. Values above 1 suggest the exposure raises risk; near 1 means little association.
hint: Put the exposed attack rate on top.

prompt: In a survey, the attack rate was 30% among people who drank the lemonade and 6% among those who did not. What is the relative risk?

options.text: 1: no association.
options.feedback: An RR near 1 would mean equal risk; this is far from 1.

options.text: 5: the drinkers were 5 times as likely to get sick.
24: the difference in attack rates.
options.feedback: That subtracts. Divide to get relative risk.

options.text: 0.2: drinkers were less likely to get ill.
options.feedback: That divides the wrong way around.

explanation: Divide, do not subtract: exposed attack rate over unexposed.
hint: Put the exposed attack rate on top.

prompt: In an outbreak, people who went to the festival have 2 times the illness of those who did not. But nearly all the sick people live in one neighborhood, and festival-goers are more common there. What is going on?

options.text: Confounding: neighborhood is linked to both festival attendance and illness, so the festival may only look related.
options.feedback: Yes: a third factor that goes with both the exposure and the illness can create a false link.

options.text: The festival is certainly the cause because the RR is high.
options.feedback: A high RR is not proof. A confounder can create the same pattern.

options.text: The data must be wrong.
options.feedback: The data may be right. The link is just not what it seems.

options.text: Neighborhood does not matter in outbreaks.
options.feedback: It matters a lot: place can be a confounder.

explanation: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome and can make a false association (or hide a real one). Checking within groups (stratifying) can reveal it.
hint: Is there something that goes with both the exposure and the illness?

prompt: A study finds that people who carry lighters get lung cancer more often. What best explains this?

options.text: Lighters cause lung cancer.
options.feedback: A lighter is a marker of smoking, not a cause.

options.text: Lung cancer causes people to buy lighters.
options.feedback: That is unlikely. The common cause is smoking.

options.text: It is just chance and cannot be explained.
options.feedback: There is a straightforward third factor.

options.text: Confounding: smoking leads people both to carry lighters and to develop lung cancer.
options.feedback: Right: carrying a lighter does not cause cancer; a third factor explains both.

explanation: A third factor connected to both exposure and illness can fake a link.
hint: Is there something that goes with both the exposure and the illness?

prompt: How can an investigator check whether neighborhood is confounding the festival-illness link?

options.text: Compare festival-goers and non-goers within each neighborhood separately.
options.feedback: Yes: stratifying by the confounder removes its influence. If the link vanishes within neighborhoods, it was confounding.

options.text: Ignore neighborhood and use more people overall.
options.feedback: More people does not remove confounding.

options.text: Trust the highest relative risk.
options.feedback: A high RR can be produced by confounding.

options.text: Remove the cases from the data.
options.feedback: Deleting cases biases the results.

explanation: Stratify by the suspected confounder. If the association disappears within strata, the confounder explains it.
hint: Look inside each group.

prompt: Cases of heat-related illness are higher in neighborhoods with more ice cream sales. How could you test whether summer weather is confounding?

options.text: Stop selling ice cream.
options.feedback: That does not test the cause.

options.text: Add more neighborhoods without any other change.
options.feedback: More data does not remove the confounder.

options.text: Assume the ice cream is the cause.
options.feedback: The link may be due to heat.

options.text: Compare ice cream sales and illness separately on hot days and on cool days.
options.feedback: Right: comparing within levels of the confounder (temperature) tests whether the link persists.

explanation: Compare within groups that share the confounder.
hint: Look inside each group.
